This page tests whether silicon sampling (Argyle et al. 2023), predicting votes using large language models (LLMs) and voter demographic information, can accurately predict the outcomes of elections. In this case, we are predicting all 35 Senate races and the chance that the Democrats get control of the US Senate in the election on November 3, 2026.

Simulated votes were created with four models: anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5, cohere/command-a-plus 🍁, moonshotai/kimi-k3 and typesafe/jev-1.14. They were all given equal weight and a multilevel logistic regression was run on the outputs to get an average impact for each of the persona features: age group, gender, race, education, party ID and state. Those impact values were then used to simulate the votes for Senator in each of the 35 states using the voting population from the 2024 CES (Schaffner et al. 2025). We then ran 10,000 simulations of the election using a normal distribution of a state error of 4.5% (a polling error of 4% combined with the model’s own uncertainty of 2.0%) and a national error of 3%. The results of our simulations and silicon samples give the Democrats a 42% chance of taking control of the Senate.

Shown above are the results of 10,000 simulations of the election based on our silicon samples. Each bar shows the share of the simulations that ended with that many seats. Bars in red represent Republicans maintaining control of the Senate, while bars in blue represent Democrats gaining control of the Senate. Along the bottom, each label shows the number of Democratic seats in blue, with the number of Republican seats in red below it. Note that in the case of 50 seats for each, control goes to the Republicans because the Republican Vice President has the deciding vote. The most likely result is 49 Democratic seats and 51 Republican seats, and 95% of the simulations had between 43 and 57 Democratic seats.


Compared with other forecasts


Chance the Democrats control the Senate                                                


Because silicon sampling is a recent technique, we compare it to other methods of predicting elections: polls (averages of the polls from VoteHub 2026, run through our simulation, with the 2024 presidential result for the 9 races without polls), betting markets (Polymarket 2026), and professional forecasters (Silver Bulletin 2026a, subscription required). The comparisons are updated daily until November 2, when the website will be frozen. Our forecast gives the Democrats a 42% chance of taking control of the Senate, which is lower than the polls at 62%, Polymarket at 74% and Silver Bulletin at 80%. One reason they might differ is that the LLMs only know the persona, the candidates and what they learned in their training, and not the latest news and campaigns (such as Trump’s historically low approval rating, see Silver Bulletin 2026b) that the polls, the betting markets and the forecasters can follow. The predictions from each of our four models are also shown, and they range from 26% (Jev) to 65% (Cohere 🍁).

In our comparison with the polls and Polymarket, most of our results agree on who is ahead. The latest poll average has a different leader from ours in only 5 of the 26 races with polls (Alaska, Georgia, Kansas, Michigan and Texas), and Polymarket in 5 of 35 (Alaska, Georgia, Kansas, Michigan and Texas). In each of them, our forecast has the Republican ahead, narrowly in all but Kansas, while the others have the Democrat ahead. More generally, our forecast leans Republican compared with the polls: our Republican share is above the poll average in 20 of the 26 races with polls. As in the comparison of the forecasts, one likely reason is that the models have a political bias despite the prompting, or that they do not know this year’s news and campaigns, which the polls and Polymarket follow. It is hard to identify the cause, since there are many parts of the method we cannot control. The actual election results may clarify some of this.
Our 95% intervals and the polls’ intervals are not comparable, because they measure two different things. Ours comes from the simulated elections, so it includes the possible polling error and the model’s own uncertainty (see Uncertainty). The polls’ interval only shows how much the polls of a race disagree with each other. It is not a margin of error, and the real result can fall outside it. The two intervals should be read with that in mind.

The poll average of a race is a weighted mean of the polls listed by VoteHub, with undecided voters left out so that the shares add up to 100%. Each poll’s weight, which we call its influence in the table, comes from four rules:

It halves every 14 days after the poll finished.
It grows with the square root of the number of people asked (up to 5,000).
It is divided by the square root of the number of polls of the race from the same pollster in the last 60 days, so that no pollster dominates.
Polls of likely voters count fully, polls of registered voters 0.8 and polls of adults 0.6.

In simple terms, an influence of 1 is about what a new poll of 600 likely voters would get, from a pollster with no other recent poll of the race. The polls’ 95% interval is the average ± 1.96 times the weighted spread of the polls around it. A Polymarket price is what traders pay for a share that pays $1 if the candidate wins, so a price of 70 cents can be read as a 70% chance of winning. We show the last price of each day.

Our forecast is more Democratic than the 2024 presidential election in most states: our Republican share is below Trump’s 2024 share in 31 of the 35 states, typically by 2.9 points. The largest moves towards the Democrats are in Delaware, Idaho, New Jersey and New Mexico. In Idaho and Nebraska, the Republican faces an independent rather than a Democrat, and the past results have no such race to compare with. The past shares are of all votes, minor candidates included, while ours are of our main candidates only, so ours are slightly higher for both sides than they would be with minor candidates. Midterm elections usually swing against the president’s party, which would push the same way. Even so, our forecast gives the Democrats less than an even chance of control, because they need to win 17 of the 35 races, and 22 of the seats up this year are held by Republicans, most of them in states Trump won.

These bars show how the models answered across all 1,050 personas, weighted by their CES weights, before the forecast model adjusts the answers to each state’s voters. On average across the four models, 40% of the answers to the Senate question were for the Republican, 34% for the Democrat and 3% for an independent; 7% were undecided and 15% would not vote. The House question gave a similar split, 41% Republican and 37% Democrat.
Jev 1.14, our only decision model, gave by far the most undecided answers (13%, against 1% to 7% for the others), and Kimi K3 the fewest. This may reflect the models’ architectures, in the terms of Thinking, Fast and Slow (Kahneman 2011). Jev 1.14 is what its makers call a “System One” model: it makes a fast, one-step judgement, picking from the options with a probability for each, and in such a quick judgement a persona’s vote may not be settled. Our other three models, Kimi K3, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Command A+ 🍁, are closer to System Two: they write their answer out word by word, taking in the whole prompt, rather than choosing in one step. Jev 1.14’s answers also varied the most from draw to draw. Because it is cheap, we took 10 draws from it instead of 3; this does not give it more weight in the forecast, since each persona’s draws from one model count once in total, but it measures its probabilities more precisely. Comparing only its first 3 draws with the other models’ 3, it gave the same answer all 3 times for 73% of personas, against 90% to 98% for the other models.

For Furkan’s approach, we chose two different kinds of model. Jev 1.14 (typesafe/jev-1.14) is a decision model: it does not write text, but gives a probability for each answer option, and each of its draws is a random pick from them. We chose it for two reasons. First, because it gives every option a probability, each option is weighed on its own, instead of the model writing out one answer. Second, it is what its makers call a “System One” model, after the fast, intuitive thinking in Thinking, Fast and Slow (Kahneman 2011): its answer is close to a person’s quick, intuitive choice, without reasoning. We wanted to see how much the chat models add on top of that, since a fast decision model could give a cheap first picture of a population. It was the cheapest model per call ($0.48 for 21,300 calls), so we took 10 draws per persona and question. Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI) is a chat model, asked 3 times at a temperature of 1.0, like Sean’s models. We chose it to see how an advanced Chinese model does on a US election; at $11.39, it was our most expensive model.
For the choice of the Anthropic and Cohere models, 15 different models from 10 companies (Anthropic, Cohere, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Mistral, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Qwen and Z.ai, all different from Furkan’s choices) were tested on 25 personas, in both question wordings and with 3 draws each, for a total cost of $0.49. Two could not be run: one because its only provider trains on the prompts it gets, which our settings block, and one because its provider did not accept the requested answer format. Of the remaining 13, Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic) and Command A+ (Cohere 🍁) were selected because they answered 100% of the time, about 90% of the Democratic and Republican personas chose their own party’s candidate, and the 3 draws gave the same answer 86% to 94% of the time. Command A+ was one of the most expensive models tested, at about $4 for a full run in the trial’s estimate, when most cost under $1. We chose Cohere 🍁 because it is Canadian, and were willing to pay more for the largest of its three models tested, since it was still well within our budget.

title: Senate Forecast 2026
text:
Methods

Data
The personas come from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (Schaffner et al. 2025), a large survey of American adults before and after the 2024 election. Its validated voters, respondents matched to a record of voting, also give the number of voters in each group. The 2022 CES (Schaffner et al. 2023) gives the same for the 2022 midterm, used only to check how much the forecast depends on whose turnout it uses. Each CES answer is stored as a code, and every code was turned into its label from the CES guide.
The candidates come from Wikipedia’s page on the 2026 Senate elections (Wikipedia contributors 2026): every Democrat and Republican, plus the four main independents (Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota). Minor-party candidates are left out, though personas can still answer “Other”. In Alaska, which uses ranked-choice voting, the forecast uses the likely final round, the Democrat against the incumbent. Past results come from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab (MIT Election Data and Science Lab 2017b, 2017a): the last Senate election for each seat and the 2024 presidential election, as shares of all votes. Wyoming’s two 2020 candidates are both labelled “Other” in the data, so we gave them their parties.
The polls come from VoteHub (VoteHub 2026): 385 general-election polls by 107 pollsters in 26 states, kept only if they ask about all of our candidates, so early polls of other possible nominees are left out. Polymarket (Polymarket 2026) gives each race’s “Senate Election Winner” market and its daily prices. Candidates’ names were matched across the sources by hand where they are written differently (Alaska has two Dan Sullivans). Every cleaned file is checked against its schema with pandera (Bantilan 2020) before it is saved. The polls and Polymarket prices are downloaded again every evening until the website is frozen on November 2.


The silicon sample
Each persona is described to the model in a system message: “You are taking part in a survey of American voters. Answer every question as the person described below would, based on who they are.”, followed by one line for each of their details (see Composition). The model is then asked the Senate question with the race’s real candidates: “The election for US Senate in [state] is on 3 November 2026. The candidates on your ballot are: [candidates]. Who will you vote for? If you have not decided, answer ‘Undecided’. If you will not vote, answer ‘Would not vote’.” It is also asked the House question, a generic ballot (Democrat, Republican or Other) used as a benchmark, and Alaska’s personas are also asked about the final round of its ranked-choice vote. Each question is its own call, and the answer must be one of the options (from a chat model, as JSON), so every answer can be read. The models were queried through OpenRouter (OpenRouter 2026).
We each ran our own approach on all 1,050 personas, with the same prompt and questions. Sean’s approach used Command A+ 🍁 (Cohere) and Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic), and Furkan’s used Jev 1.14 (TypeSafe) and Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI), so the four models come from four different companies. The chat models (all but Jev 1.14) were asked each question 3 times at a temperature of 1.0, so a persona’s answers can differ from draw to draw. Jev 1.14, a decision model, was asked 10 times, each answer a random pick from its probabilities. In all, the forecast took 40,470 answers.


From answers to a forecast
The forecast uses multilevel regression and post-stratification (MRP).
The model. Each answer for a candidate is a choice among the parties on the persona’s ballot (Democrat, Republican and, in four states, an independent), predicted from the persona’s age group, gender, race, education, party (Democrat, Republican, or independent and other) and state, in a multinomial logistic regression. Undecided, would-not-vote and missing answers are left out. The answers of all four models are pooled into one model, and each persona’s draws from one model share a weight of 1, so every model counts equally. Every group’s effect has a normal prior centred on 0 with a standard deviation of 1 (on the log-odds scale), so a group with few personas is pulled towards the average.
The frame. The 2024 CES’s validated voters, with their CES weights, give each state’s share of voters in every combination of age group, gender, race, education and party, scaled to the state’s number of votes for President in 2024.
Post-stratification. The model predicts each combination’s choice, and each state’s vote shares are these predictions weighted by the number of voters in each combination.
The simulation. We then simulate the election 10,000 times, to allow for our forecast being wrong. In each simulated election, every state’s result is shifted by two random errors. The first is a national error, the same for every state, because forecasts tend to miss in the same direction everywhere. The second is a state error, different for each state. Typically, the national error is within 3 points and the state error within 4.5 points (their standard deviations). Each error moves votes between the Republican and the other candidates: for example, an error of 2 points takes 2 points from the Republican and gives them to the others.
The candidate with the highest share wins; an independent who wins joins the Democrats with a probability of 60% to 80%, by state. Only 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up this year. The other 65 are already decided: 34 are held by Democrats or independents who vote with them, and 31 by Republicans. So in each simulated election, we add the seats each side wins to these 34 and 31. The Democrats need 51 seats to control the Senate; at 50-50, the Vice President, a Republican, breaks the tie.


Uncertainty
Our forecast has two kinds of uncertainty. The first is the model’s own: with 30 personas per state, its coefficients are not known exactly. We approximate their uncertainty with a normal distribution around the most likely coefficients (a Laplace approximation), post-stratify 1,000 draws of them, and take the standard deviation of each state’s leading share; the typical (median) state’s is 2.0%.
The second is the possible polling error, the error of the method itself. Even a well-estimated forecast can miss the real result: some voters change their minds before election day, and the people who turn out to vote may differ from those we expected. Silicon sampling has no past elections to check how far off it can be, so we assume errors of the size election forecasts usually make: a few points in each state, often in the same direction everywhere. We chose 4 points for each state and 3 points for the whole country. Combined with the model’s own 2 points, the error in each state is about 4.5 points.
Each of our 95% intervals covers the middle 95% of the 10,000 simulated elections, and a chance of winning is the share of simulated elections a candidate wins. The polls’ 95% interval only shows how much the polls disagree with each other.

title: Senate Forecast 2026
text:
Discussion
Our silicon sampling method gives the Democrats only a 42% chance of taking control of the Senate, while all the comparisons (polls, betting markets, professional forecasters) give the Democrats between a 62% and 80% chance. Is our method picking up something all the others are missing, or is our method just not reliable enough? One reason to doubt our method is that our four LLMs disagree on the odds, from 26% (Jev) to 65% (Cohere 🍁). Note that the combined forecast is not simply the average of the four models’ predictions; rather, the answers are pooled before the MRP (see the Methods section).
All of these forecasts are uncertain. Our 42% chance is not far from a coin flip, and 95% of our simulations had between 43 and 57 Democratic seats. Most of that uncertainty comes from the possible polling error of 4% in each state, not the models’ own uncertainty of 2.0%. Silver Bulletin’s 80% still gives the Republicans about a one-in-five chance of keeping the Senate, and its seat distribution, like ours, spreads across several seats on both sides of 50 (Silver Bulletin 2026a). One election cannot prove which forecast was better: a 20% or 42% chance happens often. The results of all 35 races on November 3 will be a better test than control alone.
In particular, our predictions differ from both the polls and the betting market in five states: Texas, Alaska, Georgia, Michigan and Kansas (see Race by race). In the first four, we give the Republican only a 52% to 61% chance of winning, so they are close races for us too, and in Kansas a 78% chance. If the Democrats win three of these five and every other race goes as we predict, they would have 51 seats and control of the Senate, which is what the polls and the betting market are predicting. If they win all five, they would have 53 seats, the average in the Silver Bulletin forecast (Silver Bulletin 2026a).
If the silicon sampling turns out to be inaccurate when compared to the election results, there are three plausible explanations. The first is that we did not include any news or current political climate in our prompts, and the models selected may not have been trained with recent information. In contrast, the other forecasts do take into account Trump’s low popularity ratings (Silver Bulletin 2026b) and issues that voters have said are important, like corruption and the price of gas and groceries (CNBC 2026). A second cause is that we are using turnout from the 2024 presidential election, which had high Republican turnout and was not a midterm election. We also ran the simulation using 2022 turnout (Schaffner et al. 2023), the most recent midterm election, but it did not significantly change the prediction: the Democrats’ chance of control went from 42% to 41%. The last midterm election when a Republican was president was 2018, but we decided this election was too old to use. The third plausible explanation is that LLMs may simply not be good predictors of how people vote. Argyle et al. (2023) found that GPT-3 could reproduce how groups of Americans voted, which they called “algorithmic fidelity”, and in our trial about 90% of the Democratic and Republican personas chose their own party’s candidate. However, more recent work finds that LLMs tend to flatten people into stereotypes (Bisbee et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024). We think of each answer as a stereotype with a little noise added: in our trial, the three draws gave the same answer 86% to 94% of the time, and Bisbee et al. (2024) also found that the answers change with the model, as ours do.
The big advantage of silicon sampling is that it is much cheaper than polling. On the other hand, betting market prices are free to read, and markets have often predicted elections better than polls (Wolfers and Zitzewitz 2004), so they may turn out to be a better and cheaper alternative to silicon sampling. The election on November 3 will be the first real test of our method against both polling and betting markets.

Limitations
The choices we made while building our method mean some things were left out or limited, and these could be added or enhanced in future work to check their impact. These limitations are the lack of current news, our choice of low- and mid-priced models, and our decision to try only two wordings of the prompt.
The first limitation is that the prompts were not given any information about the current political climate, which might have shifted the responses. However, even by adding recent news and information about the political climate, we would still have to decide which news sources, what types of news to include, and if each persona should get the same news or different news to reflect their political leaning. Murray and Alexander (2026) found that the news given to the model changed the Democratic share by about 10 percentage points, but had little effect when the persona included political identity, as ours do with party ID. All of these could be important factors, and testing all of them would be considerably more expensive in LLM costs.
A second limitation is that we used models that were either cheap or moderate in price. More expensive models may have more accurate results, either because their training data is more recent or because they are better at detecting voting pattern changes from election to election. Our main reason for not choosing more expensive models was price. We asked the two most expensive models on OpenRouter the same Senate question three times, and estimated that one full run of our approach (6,390 calls) would cost about $3,000 for GPT-5.5 Pro and $42 for Claude Fable 5.1, against $11 for Kimi K3 and $3.52 for Cohere’s Command A+ 🍁.
The final limitation that could be addressed with future work is varying the prompt. Heath and Alexander (2026) found that asking for political opinions in the model’s own words, then mapping the text to a numeric scale, gives distributions of answers that more closely fit real respondents’ than asking for a number. Different prompts could be tested to get better distributions of votes, which might lead to more accurate predictions.
As Murray and Alexander (2026) found, the choice of model, persona detail, news and prompt style together could move the Democratic share anywhere from 0 to 100%, so any change to the method should be checked against real election results. We will wait for the results on November 3, 2026 before trying any of these changes, so we can first see how accurate the current method is.
